name: Wide / establishing shot
purpose: Orients the viewer in the space before anything happens; shows full body plus surroundings so a viewer can copy a movement or judge scale.
when_to_use: Opening shot of a tutorial or demo; any moment you need the audience to see the whole setup (e.g. a home-workout routine in a small room).
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy (Michael Wiese Productions, 2009)

name: Medium shot
purpose: Balances context and facial expression; the default 'talking and doing' shot.
when_to_use: Main narration/demo shots where you need to see both the presenter's face and their hands/body doing something.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Close-up
purpose: Heightens emotional intensity or draws attention to a specific detail (face, product, hands).
when_to_use: Emotional beats, product reveals, or 'watch exactly how I do this' form-check moments.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Extreme close-up
purpose: Isolates one detail to create tension, curiosity, or precision (an eye, an ingredient, a number on a screen).
when_to_use: Hook moments in the first 3 seconds, or a single critical detail (a mistake, a result number).
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Point-of-view (POV) shot
purpose: Puts the viewer directly in the subject's perspective, increasing immersion and empathy.
when_to_use: Showing 'what you'll see when you do this' in a tutorial, or building suspense in a story-driven video.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Over-the-shoulder shot
purpose: Frames a conversation or demonstration from behind one participant, keeping both people connected in-frame.
when_to_use: Interviews, two-person dialogue, or a 'watching someone do something' teaching moment.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Low angle
purpose: Camera looks up at the subject, making them appear powerful, confident, or dominant.
when_to_use: Authority-building moments (a coach demonstrating expertise, a confident brand statement).
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: High angle
purpose: Camera looks down at the subject, making them appear smaller, vulnerable, or relatable.
when_to_use: Showing struggle, vulnerability, or a 'before' state in a transformation story.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Dutch / tilted angle
purpose: Tilts the horizon to create unease, disorientation, or energy.
when_to_use: Comedic beats, chaotic moments, or 'something's off' storytelling cues. Use sparingly — overuse reads as amateurish.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Dolly-in / push-in
purpose: Camera moves slowly toward the subject, building emotional intensity and drawing the viewer into a moment.
when_to_use: Reveal moments, emotional peaks, or the climax of a mistake/lesson story.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Dolly-out / pull-out
purpose: Camera moves away from the subject, revealing context or creating a sense of resolution.
when_to_use: Ending shots, revealing the full result of a transformation, or comedic context-reveals.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Tracking / follow shot
purpose: Camera moves alongside the subject, maintaining energy and continuity of action.
when_to_use: Walk-and-talk intros, action B-roll, or following a process from start to finish.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Handheld
purpose: Slight camera instability reads as authentic, urgent, or 'in the moment' — the opposite of polished.
when_to_use: Vlogging, behind-the-scenes segments, or moments meant to feel raw/unscripted.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Static / locked-off shot
purpose: A perfectly still frame lets the action or performance carry the shot without camera distraction.
when_to_use: Tutorial demonstration shots where the viewer needs to study the movement without camera noise.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Whip pan
purpose: A fast, blurred camera swing that creates an energetic or comedic transition between two shots.
when_to_use: Fast-paced cuts between scenes, comedic beats, or high-energy Shorts/Reels editing.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Cutaway / insert shot
purpose: A brief shot of a supporting detail (hands, an object, a phone screen) that adds information without breaking the main shot's continuity.
when_to_use: Showing an ingredient, a product feature, or a step's result while the main narration continues.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Reaction shot
purpose: Shows a person's emotional response to something just seen or said, building empathy and pacing.
when_to_use: Testimonial moments, comedic timing, or letting a 'wow' reaction sell a result.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

name: Two-shot
purpose: Frames two people together in one shot, visually establishing their relationship or dynamic.
when_to_use: Collaboration content, interviews, or family/relationship-driven storytelling.
further_reading: Master Shots by Christopher Kenworthy

definition: People feel obligated to return a favor or value they've received.
hook_application: Give the viewer something useful (a tip, a laugh, a free resource) before asking for a follow, like, or purchase — the 'jab before the right hook' idea.
further_reading: Influence by Robert Cialdini (HarperBusiness); Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk

definition: People assign more value to things that are limited in availability or time.
hook_application: Time-boxed or limited-availability framing in a hook or CTA ('only works for the next 24 hours', 'limited spots').
further_reading: Influence by Robert Cialdini

definition: People are more easily persuaded by sources they perceive as credible or expert.
hook_application: Open with a credential you hold, a demonstrated result you achieved, or the source of your expertise before giving advice - signals the video is worth trusting.
further_reading: Influence by Robert Cialdini

definition: People look to others' behavior to decide what's correct, especially under uncertainty.
hook_application: Showing real comments, results from your own audience, or testimonials builds trust fast in a hook. Only cite numbers ('X people tried this') if you have the actual data - never estimate.
further_reading: Influence by Robert Cialdini

definition: People are more easily persuaded by people they like or feel similar to.
hook_application: Relatable framing, shared identity/language (local slang, regional dialect), humor, and authenticity increase a hook's pull.
further_reading: Influence by Robert Cialdini

definition: Once people commit to something small, they feel pressure to act consistently with that commitment.
hook_application: Small early CTAs ('comment DAY 1', 'save this for later') build toward larger asks (subscribe, buy) later in a series.
further_reading: Influence by Robert Cialdini

definition: Shared group identity ('people like us') deepens persuasion beyond simple liking.
hook_application: Framing content around a shared identity ('for Mumbai flat-dwellers', 'for working moms') increases relevance and trust.
further_reading: Influence by Robert Cialdini (added in later editions)

steps: Character (the audience is the hero)
Problem (external, internal, philosophical)
Guide (the brand, positioned as mentor not hero)
Plan (a clear, simple path forward)
Call to action
Success (what happens if they follow the plan)
Failure (what happens if they don't)
video_application: Frame the creator/brand as the guide and the viewer as the hero with a problem; the video becomes the 'plan', the CTA is explicit, and showing both the payoff and the cost of inaction increases follow-through.

steps: State the problem the audience has
Agitate it — make the pain concrete and immediate
Solve it with your content/product
video_application: Classic short-form hook structure: name the pain point in the first line, twist the knife briefly, then deliver the fix — works especially well for 'mistake' and 'myth-busting' video formats.

steps: Show the 'before' state (the struggle)
Show the 'after' state (the transformation/result)
Show the 'bridge' — how to get from one to the other
video_application: Ideal for transformation content (fitness, skincare, home organization) — open on the after/result to hook curiosity, then walk back to show the bridge.

steps: Setup (introduce character/situation)
Confrontation (the obstacle or complication)
Resolution (the outcome)
video_application: Even a 60-second video benefits from a compressed 3-act shape: a few seconds of setup, the bulk of the video on the obstacle/attempt, and a clear payoff at the end.

steps: Monitor breaking news/trends in your niche
Move fast — the window is hours, not days
Attach your brand/expertise to the trend with a genuine angle, not a forced tie-in
video_application: React to a trending topic in your niche (a viral claim, a new product, a seasonal event) within the trend's live window to capture algorithmic reach that evergreen content can't get on its own.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott (Wiley)

steps: Define the specific audience segment (not 'everyone')
Identify their language, pain points, and platform habits
Tailor the story's problem/solution to that exact segment
video_application: The more specific the audience, the easier it is to speak to them. 'Home workouts for small city flats' speaks to a clearer group than 'fitness', because those viewers share the same limits (little space, busy days). Decide who you're talking to, then shape the problem and the fix for that group.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott

steps: Publish directly to your audience instead of relying on gatekeepers (press, algorithms alone)
Build owned channels (email list, community) alongside platform reach
Use consistency and authenticity over polish
video_application: Encourages creators to treat YouTube/Instagram as a direct relationship channel — consistent posting and community reply builds compounding trust beyond any single video's performance.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott

steps: Exposition (setup)
Rising action (building complication)
Climax (peak tension/turning point)
Falling action (consequences unfold)
Resolution (final outcome)
video_application: A more granular alternative to the 3-act structure for longer-form videos (5-10+ min) — gives two extra beats (rising/falling action) to build and release tension around a demonstration or story.
further_reading: Academic narrative theory; referenced in Storytelling: A Strategic Approach (Monique Schröder, Copenhagen Business School, 2015)

steps: Hero — the one with the goal (your viewer)
Mentor/Guide — the one who helps (your brand/creator)
Threshold/obstacle — what stands in the way
video_application: Mirrors StoryBrand's Character+Guide structure; useful when scripting a video as a mini-journey rather than a flat list of tips — gives the viewer a role to see themselves in.
further_reading: Joseph Campbell's monomyth; referenced in Storytelling: A Strategic Approach (Monique Schröder, 2015)

steps: Draw the viewer into a story world (vivid, specific detail)
Reduce their critical/skeptical distance while 'inside' the story
Deliver the message/CTA while transportation is highest
video_application: Explains why a specific, concrete anecdote ('I tried this for 30 days and...') out-persuades a generic claim — specificity increases immersion, which increases persuasion.
further_reading: Narrative transportation theory (Green & Brock); referenced in Storytelling: A Strategic Approach (Monique Schröder, 2015)

template: [Action], ghar pe/apne shehar mein, bina [barrier], sirf [duration] minute — chalo shuru
[Pain point] ka time ya resource nahi hai?
Ye [number] galtiyan tumhara [outcome] kharab kar rahi hain
[Common belief] band karo. Iske bajaye [alternative] karo.
[Number] logo ne yeh try kiya — result dekho
[Number]% log yeh galat karte hain — sahi tareeka yeh hai

definition: Very specific niche topics can reach a small, exact audience directly online; an audience doesn't have to be huge to matter.
video_application: Instead of broad topics, try a precise one, like 'budget skincare for tier-2 city students' rather than 'skincare tips'. Fewer people search for it, but the ones who do find a video made for their exact problem.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott, Ch. 2

definition: Publishing genuine expertise directly to your audience (rather than through media gatekeepers) builds long-term trust and authority.
video_application: A creator who consistently teaches real, useful expertise builds compounding channel trust that outlasts any single viral hit — supports prioritizing a content pillar/series strategy over one-off videos.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott, Ch. 3

definition: Actively tracking what's said about you across social platforms and blogs surfaces both opportunities (trending questions) and problems (complaints) early.
video_application: Creators should monitor their own comments and niche conversations to catch a recurring question or complaint that can become the next video topic — a low-cost, high-relevance content-idea source.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott, Ch. 5

definition: Content spreads virally when several independent communities each find their own reason to share it around the same time, rather than from one single push or channel.
video_application: Design a video to give multiple distinct audiences (e.g. fitness beginners AND busy parents AND budget-conscious viewers) their own reason to share it, instead of targeting only one angle.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott, Ch. 8

definition: The depth and usefulness of an entire content ecosystem — not any single polished asset — drives discoverability and credibility.
video_application: Supports the series/playlist strategy over isolated videos: a channel with a deep, organized back-catalog on a niche out-performs one with scattered unrelated uploads, both for search and for viewer trust.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott, Ch. 9

definition: The same core story or message is adapted across multiple formats (blog, audio, video, forum discussion) to meet different audiences where their consumption habits already are.
video_application: Repurpose one core hook/story across YouTube long-form, Shorts, and community posts so the same message reinforces itself across touchpoints instead of existing only once.
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR by David Meerman Scott, Ch. 4-6

definition: Every brand or creator has an underlying 'why' — the founding reason and values behind what they do — and this core story should ground every piece of content, even when only a simplified version is shown externally.
video_application: Before scripting individual videos, define your channel's one-sentence 'why' (e.g. 'I make fitness accessible for people with no time or equipment'). Every video's hook and CTA should trace back to that core story so the channel feels coherent over time, not like disconnected one-offs.
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach by Monique Schröder (Copenhagen Business School, 2015), citing Fog et al. 2010

definition: Organizations (and by extension creators) tell a simple, external-facing story day-to-day, while a more complex internal story explains the full context of decisions and direction.
video_application: The short hook/caption is your 'operational' story (simple, external); your channel's about section or a longer-form video can carry the fuller 'strategic' story of why you make this content — keep both consistent with each other.
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach by Monique Schröder, citing Madsen-Mygdal 2014

definition: Storytelling in an organization serves four distinct functions: internal leadership (aligning a team around shared values), marketing communication (engaging an audience emotionally), external stakeholder narratives (how others talk about you, which you don't fully control), and cultural sensemaking (helping people understand their own identity through the story).
video_application: A creator's storytelling operates in at least two of these lanes: marketing communication (the video itself) and cultural sensemaking (why the audience relates to and shares it) — a video that only sells but doesn't help the audience make sense of their own situation misses the sensemaking function that drives sharing.
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach by Monique Schröder, Ch. 3.3.1

definition: A brand or piece of content becomes more meaningful to someone the more closely it connects to their own sense of identity — people process content partly to satisfy their own psychological need to make sense of their world.
video_application: Content that helps a viewer understand their own situation (e.g. 'why you're always tired even after 8 hours of sleep') creates a deeper connection than content that only demonstrates a product or skill, because it ties into the viewer's self-understanding.
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach by Monique Schröder, citing Escalas 2004

principle: Story building blocks (audience, message, conflict, character, plot, action)
definition: Across the literature, the recurring elements needed for an effective story are: a clearly understood target audience, a clear message, a conflict/challenge, relatable characters, a plot, and a resulting action.
video_application: A practical pre-shoot checklist: name your audience specifically, state your one message in a sentence, name the conflict/pain point, decide who the 'character' is (usually the viewer or the creator), sketch the plot beats, and confirm the action you want the viewer to take.
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach by Monique Schröder, Ch. 5.2.3

principle: Repetition as the true success signal
definition: Genuine storytelling success isn't just the audience showing interest once — it's when they repeat or retell the story themselves, which signals real engagement and impact.
video_application: Track not just views/likes but whether viewers repeat your framing in comments, duets, or their own captions — that's a stronger signal of a hook or story actually landing than raw view count alone.
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach by Monique Schröder, Ch. 5.2.4, citing Mills 2008

concept: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook framework
definition: A boxing metaphor for content cadence: 'jabs' are lightweight, generous content that entertains/engages without asking for anything (builds the relationship), while the 'right hook' is the direct call to action/sales ask. Most content should be jabs; the right hook only lands well after enough jabs have built trust.
video_application: Plan a content calendar where most videos give pure value with no ask (comedy, tips, entertainment) and only occasionally does a video carry a direct CTA — matches the earlier commitment/consistency and reciprocity persuasion principles already in this dataset.
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk (HarperBusiness, 2013)

definition: Content is tailored to the specific culture, format, and language norms of the platform it's posted on, rather than reposting the same asset everywhere.
video_application: A hook that works as on-screen text on a Reel may need a completely different pacing/format as a YouTube Short or a long-form intro — don't just resize the same video across platforms.
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk

definition: Effective content blends into the viewer's normal browsing/entertainment experience and feels like part of the conversation, not an ad breaking into it.
video_application: Open videos the way the platform's native creators talk to their audience, not the way a traditional TV ad opens — avoid a 'commercial' tone in the first few seconds.
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk

definition: Most content should be generous — giving value, entertainment, or community connection — without an ask attached; overwhelming the audience with sales pitches erodes trust.
video_application: Reserve explicit CTAs for a minority of videos; let most videos simply deliver on the hook's promise without pivoting to a sales ask.
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk

definition: Content that connects to current trends or shared cultural moments feels timely and relatable, increasing engagement.
video_application: Pairs with the earlier 'newsjacking' concept — tie a niche topic to something currently trending in the broader culture when there's a genuine, non-forced connection.
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk

definition: Small, timely, culturally-relevant snippets keep a brand or creator agile and able to react quickly, rather than relying only on big, infrequent productions.
video_application: Favor a steady stream of short, timely videos/Shorts alongside occasional bigger productions — agility beats a slow, over-produced release schedule.
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk

definition: Content reinforces a recognizable identity across platforms and stays aware of the brand's/creator's own tone and limits, rather than chasing every trend regardless of fit.
video_application: Ties to the earlier core-story principle — every video, hook, and CTA should feel recognizably 'you' even as formats vary by platform.
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk

note: Visual-first, closed-loop-sharing platforms are well-suited to establishing brand story and identity ('jabs') but make a direct call-to-action harder to execute smoothly — CTAs need to feel native (e.g. 'link in bio', a caption prompt) rather than an overt sales push in the visual itself.
video_application: On Reels/Instagram, put more weight on visual storytelling and identity-building; move harder CTAs to captions, bio links, or a dedicated occasional post rather than forcing them into every visual.
source: general_marketing_knowledge (platform specifics like exact algorithms have changed since 2013; verify current mechanics separately)
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk, Ch. 6

jab_hook_balance: engagement unlocks reach for the hook
note: On algorithmic feed platforms, engagement on 'jab' content increases the algorithm's willingness to show later 'right hook' content — engagement is a prerequisite, not a side effect.
video_application: Build engagement habits (comments, shares) with value-first content before posting a conversion-focused video, so the platform's distribution system already favors your channel.
source: general_marketing_knowledge (specific algorithm names like EdgeRank are outdated; the underlying principle — engagement gates reach — still generally applies)
further_reading: Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook by Gary Vaynerchuk, Ch. 3

guidance: ASCI asks for a clear, upfront disclosure label - such as 'Ad' or 'Paid partnership' - visible without needing to click 'more'. Use the platform's own paid-partnership tool as well as an on-screen label. Guidelines are updated periodically, so check ASCI's current version before posting.
video_application: Put the label on screen as on-screen text from the start of the video, not only in the caption, and keep it up for as long as ASCI's current guidelines ask for a video of your length. Write it in the same language as the video. Also turn on the platform's paid-partnership tag.
further_reading: ASCI Influencer Guidelines PDF, ascionline.in

guidance: Good practice (reflected in CCPA endorsement guidance) is to only endorse a product or service you have actually used or experienced yourself, not just repeated brand claims. If a brand hasn't sent you the product, ask for it before agreeing to the deal.
video_application: Base the script on your own hands-on experience with the product - an actual first impression or usage moment on camera - rather than reading out brand-supplied claims you haven't verified yourself.
source: Department of Consumer Affairs, 'Endorsement Know-hows!' (Jan 2023), checked 2026-09-21
further_reading: PIB Press Release on CCPA Guidelines, pib.gov.in

guidance: On Influora, the brand has 3 working days to review your draft - after that, the Influora team steps in. You get up to 2 rounds of revisions. Once it's approved, post it live and share the link on Influora; you're paid by bank transfer within 2 working days of that live link.
video_application: Plan your shoot-to-post schedule around this flow: submit drafts with enough runway for the 3-working-day review, use your revision rounds to align with feedback, then post live and share the link on Influora promptly since that link starts the payment countdown.

topic: Health and finance content need disclosed expertise
guidance: For health, nutrition, banking, finance or insurance content, ASCI asks that technical advice or claims (a treatment, cure, prevention, returns, a specific investment) come only from creators who hold the relevant qualification and show it upfront; for stocks or investments that includes a SEBI registration number. General, non-technical mentions usually don't need this. Check ASCI's current guidelines for your case.
video_application: Without the relevant qualification, keep a health or finance brand video general (for example, why regular check-ups matter) and make no treatment, cure or returns claim, not even as 'it worked for me'. If you are qualified, show it on screen at the start.
source: ASCI influencer guidelines, Addendum 2 (17 Aug 2023), checked 2026-09-21
further_reading: ASCI Influencer Guidelines PDF, ascionline.in

topic: Disclosure required even for genuine reviews
guidance: ASCI asks for a disclosure label whenever there's a material connection with a brand (a free product, payment or other benefit), even when your review is completely genuine. Saying 'I wasn't paid for this' doesn't replace the label if you did get something. Check ASCI's current guidelines.
video_application: Add the disclosure label any time a brand gave you the product free or paid you for the video, no matter how independent or positive your actual opinion is - disclosure is about the connection, not the verdict.

hook_angle: Open on the visible result or a common misconception, then walk back to show how you got there or why it's wrong.
never_say: No medical, treatment or 'cure' claims (acne, pigmentation, hair fall), even framed as 'it worked for me', unless you hold and show a relevant qualification. No 'clinically proven' language and no promised result timelines.
source: Influora research on Indian beauty/skincare-creator formats, compiled 2026-09-21; claim limits per ASCI guidelines

hook_angle: Open on the finished look or a 'how do I style this' question, then show the transformation or breakdown.
never_say: No unverified claims about fabric quality or 'cheapest / best price' comparisons, and no promotion of counterfeit or replica products.
source: Influora research on Indian fashion-creator formats, compiled 2026-09-21

hook_angle: Open on the finished dish or the most visually striking step, then walk through how you got there.
never_say: No medical or 'cures' / 'boosts immunity' claims, no 'clinically proven' language, and no specific nutrition numbers unless you can cite a real source. Say 'this is what worked for me' when sharing a personal experience.
source: Influora research on Indian food-creator formats, compiled 2026-09-21

formats: What I eat in a day
hook_angle: Open with the movement or result the viewer wants, then show the how - including proper form.
never_say: No weight-loss-in-X-days claims, before/after promises or guaranteed results, and no diet, supplement or injury advice unless you hold and show a relevant qualification. No medical, 'cure' or 'clinically proven' claims. Say 'this is my routine', not 'this will work for you'.
source: Influora research on Indian fitness-creator formats, compiled 2026-09-21; claim limits per ASCI guidelines

hook_angle: Open on the product reveal or the single most surprising feature, then move into the full evaluation.
never_say: No unverified performance claims ('fastest', 'best') and no misleading comparisons that favor a sponsor. Disclose the partnership clearly regardless of how the review reads.
source: Influora research on Indian tech/gadgets-creator formats, compiled 2026-09-21

hook_angle: Open with a relatable money habit or question, then walk through the practical fix.
never_say: No stock or fund tips, no 'guaranteed returns', and nothing framed as personal financial advice. ASCI asks for a SEBI registration number for stock or investment content, and SEBI has rules on which creators regulated brands (brokers, fund houses) may work with; check the current SEBI and ASCI guidelines before any finance deal. Keep market data general, not tied to recent prices.
source: Influora research on Indian personal finance-creator formats, compiled 2026-09-21; claim limits per SEBI/ASCI guidelines

hook_angle: Open on the most visually striking destination moment, then walk through the practical how-to-get-there details.
never_say: No absolute safety claims ('completely safe') and no cost claims without noting prices can change over time. Disclose sponsored stays or hotels clearly.
source: Influora research on Indian travel-creator formats, compiled 2026-09-21

hook_angle: Open straight into the exaggerated or relatable moment - no setup - then let the punchline land.
never_say: No mocking real, identifiable individuals without consent, no content that could read as misinformation dressed as satire, and disclose clearly when a sketch is a paid brand integration.
source: Influora research on Indian comedy/entertainment-creator formats, compiled 2026-09-21

hook_angle: Open with a relatable parenting moment or question, then share what worked for your family.
never_say: No medical advice for children, and no showing children's private details (school name, face-identifiable location, full name in text). Say 'this is what worked for us' rather than framing any one method as the only right way.
source: Influora research on Indian parenting-creator formats, compiled 2026-09-21; claim limits per ASCI guidelines

hook_angle: Open with the transformed space or the most satisfying moment of the routine, then walk through how you got there.
never_say: No claims about productivity or lifestyle changes guaranteeing specific outcomes, and no promotion of expensive products as 'must-haves'. Say 'this is what worked for me' when sharing personal routines.
source: Influora research on Indian lifestyle-creator formats, compiled 2026-09-21

hook_angle: Open with a relatable wellness struggle or question, then share what helped you personally.
never_say: No medical claims, no 'cure' or 'treat' language for any health condition, no 'clinically proven' statements, and no diagnosis or treatment advice. Mental health content should encourage professional help when needed. Say 'this helped me' rather than prescribing solutions.
source: Influora research on Indian wellness-creator formats, compiled 2026-09-21; claim limits per ASCI guidelines

hook_angle: Open with the most exciting gameplay moment or the problem you're solving, then show the strategy.
never_say: No promotion of real-money gaming, betting, or gambling platforms. ASCI has specific guidelines on gaming and betting advertising - check the current version before posting any gaming content that involves stakes or rewards. No promises about winning or earning through games.
source: Influora research on Indian gaming-creator formats, compiled 2026-09-21; claim limits per ASCI guidelines

hook_angle: Open with a common study struggle or question, then walk through the practical technique or resource.
never_say: No guaranteed marks, scores, ranks, or job placement promises. No 'crack any exam' or 'guaranteed selection' language. Focus on study techniques and resources that helped you personally, not promised outcomes.
source: Influora research on Indian education-creator formats, compiled 2026-09-21; claim limits per ASCI guidelines

note: A strong first moment and viewers watching to the end matter more than hitting any particular length. Treat this as a general shape, not a formula; Instagram changes how Reels are shown.
video_application: Put your strongest visual or line first, add on-screen text for sound-off viewers, and cut anything that doesn't earn its place before the payoff - design for full watch-throughs and shares rather than chasing a specific length.
source: Influora general guidance, checked 2026-09-21; platform mechanics change

note: Sticking to one clear theme and a steady posting rhythm makes a channel easier for viewers to understand and come back to. Treat this as a general pattern, not a formula.
video_application: Pick one clear theme for a run of Shorts before branching out, and pair Shorts with occasional longer videos on the same topic rather than posting unrelated one-offs.
source: Influora general guidance, checked 2026-09-21; platform mechanics change

template: [Action], at home or in your city, without [barrier] - let's start
The mistakes that are quietly ruining your [outcome]
People tried this - see what happened
Most people get this wrong - here's the right way

name: Color spot
purpose: Dressing a subject or key prop in one standout color against a plainer background makes them instantly recognizable, even blurred or distant.
when_to_use: Helping a viewer track a specific person, product or team color across a busy or fast-cut sequence.
source: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques, Christopher Kenworthy, Michael Wiese Productions, 2009

name: Sharp subject, soft crowd
purpose: Keeping only the main subject in sharp focus and better lit than everyone else around them makes them the obvious point of interest in a busy scene.
when_to_use: Market, event, or street content where you want your subject (or a specific person/product) to stand out from a crowded background.
source: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques, Christopher Kenworthy, Michael Wiese Productions, 2009

name: Step into the light
purpose: Letting the subject walk from shadow into light, with the camera tilting up as their face becomes visible, gives a simple arrival real weight.
when_to_use: An entrance moment for a person, a transformation reveal, or the start of a dramatic story segment.
source: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques, Christopher Kenworthy, Michael Wiese Productions, 2009

name: Turn-and-approach
purpose: Starting with the subject walking away, then turning to walk straight at the camera, signals a change of mind or a new decision without needing narration.
when_to_use: A 'then I decided...' beat in a storytime video, or a transition into a confident brand statement.
source: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques, Christopher Kenworthy, Michael Wiese Productions, 2009

name: Low-to-wide reveal
purpose: Starting tight and low, then panning and moving behind the subject as they crouch or stop, reveals a much bigger space or challenge than the audience expected.
when_to_use: Showing the true scale of a task, a crowd, or a venue right after a close, secretive-feeling opening.
source: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques, Christopher Kenworthy, Michael Wiese Productions, 2009

name: Mirror reveal
purpose: A mirror in frame lets a second subject or detail appear and be noticed in the same shot, without cutting away and back.
when_to_use: Getting-ready or room-tour content where something (a person, a mess, a surprise) is revealed through a mirror behind you.
source: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques, Christopher Kenworthy, Michael Wiese Productions, 2009

name: Open-and-reveal
purpose: Builds anticipation by hiding the subject behind a closed door, box, curtain or bag, then opening it to reveal them or the product centered in frame.
when_to_use: Product unboxings, outfit reveals, or 'guess what's inside' openers where the opening itself is the hook.
source: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques, Christopher Kenworthy, Michael Wiese Productions, 2009

name: Parting reveal
purpose: Two people or objects that start blocking the view move apart like curtains, opening up the frame to show what was hidden behind them.
when_to_use: A crowd or group parting to reveal a product, guest, or result -- works well as a mid-video payoff beat.
source: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques, Christopher Kenworthy, Michael Wiese Productions, 2009

name: Walk-in behind you
purpose: Lets something important appear behind the main subject while the front of the frame barely moves, so the audience discovers it themselves instead of being told about it.
when_to_use: A 'wait for it' reel where a person, pet, or product quietly walks into frame behind you while you keep talking to camera.
source: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques, Christopher Kenworthy, Michael Wiese Productions, 2009

name: Follow-the-object pan
purpose: Following a handed-off or carried object as it moves gives the camera a natural reason to pan from one person or area to another, instead of an random camera movement with no clear reason.
when_to_use: Moving between two people or setups in one continuous shot -- for example following a product as it's passed to a friend for a reaction.
source: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: Master Shots: 100 Advanced Camera Techniques, Christopher Kenworthy, Michael Wiese Productions, 2009

definition: Writing that leans on vague, inflated buzzwords instead of specific, everyday language actually tells the audience less, not more, and makes the message sound like every other pitch.
video_application: Drop words like 'premium quality', 'game-changing' or 'must-have' in captions and voiceovers. Say exactly what the product does and for whom, the way you'd explain it to a friend, so it's clear instead of generic-sounding.
source: The New Rules of Marketing and PR (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR, David Meerman Scott, 2010

concept: Match the words people actually search
definition: Content gets found when its title and description use the same specific words and phrases the audience types into search, not clever or vague alternatives that only make sense internally.
video_application: Title and caption a Reel or YouTube video with the plain phrase a viewer would type ('easy hostel breakfast recipe') rather than a witty pun, so the title matches what people looking for that need actually search.
source: The New Rules of Marketing and PR (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR, David Meerman Scott, 2010

concept: Plan a series, not one-off posts
definition: Treating content as an ongoing plan built around what the audience needs to know keeps topics connected and easier to follow than deciding each post on the day.
video_application: Before filming, note the questions your followers keep asking and line up a short run of videos that answer them in order, instead of deciding each video's topic the morning you post it.
source: The New Rules of Marketing and PR (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR, David Meerman Scott, 2010

concept: Decide the goal before you script the content
definition: Effective content starts from a clear, specific action you want the viewer to take, and works backward from that action to the story - not the other way around.
video_application: Before writing a script, decide whether this particular video is meant to get saves, drive DMs, or send people to a link, and shape the hook, body and closing line around that one goal.
source: The New Rules of Marketing and PR (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR, David Meerman Scott, 2010

concept: Go deep on a few platforms instead of everywhere
definition: Spreading the same effort across every available platform usually produces weaker results than focusing on the handful of platforms where your specific audience already spends its time.
video_application: Rather than posting a weaker version of every video to five apps, pick the one or two platforms your audience actually watches on and put your full editing and posting effort there.
source: The New Rules of Marketing and PR (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR, David Meerman Scott, 2010

concept: Tailor every application instead of copy-pasting
definition: A generic message sent to many people reads as spam and is easy to ignore; a short message that shows you actually looked at the other person's work is far more likely to be read.
video_application: When you apply to a campaign on Influora, mention something specific about that brand's product or brief in your pitch instead of reusing the same text for every campaign. The same goes for asking another creator to collab.
source: The New Rules of Marketing and PR (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR, David Meerman Scott, 2010

characteristic: Replying to real questions is part of the content, not an afterthought
definition: Answering questions and comments in your niche - on your own posts and elsewhere - is itself a form of content that builds presence and surfaces ideas for future videos.
video_application: Set aside time to genuinely answer comments and questions in your niche's community, and keep a running note of questions that repeat - each one is a candidate for a future video topic.
source: The New Rules of Marketing and PR (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR, David Meerman Scott, 2010

characteristic: One clear next step, not several vague asks
definition: When a piece of content does include a call to action, it works best as a single, specific instruction rather than a list of options that makes the viewer choose.
video_application: If a video ends with an ask, make it one thing - 'comment your city' or 'save this for later' - instead of stacking follow, comment, share and link-in-bio into the same closing line.
source: The New Rules of Marketing and PR (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR, David Meerman Scott, 2010

characteristic: Improves through testing and response, not a fixed first draft
definition: Content that performs well over time usually got there by being adjusted based on how the audience actually reacted, rather than being planned to perfection before the first post.
video_application: Treat your first version of a format (a series intro, a caption style) as a draft: watch how comments and watch-time respond, then adjust the next one instead of repeating the same approach unchanged.
source: The New Rules of Marketing and PR (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: The New Rules of Marketing and PR, David Meerman Scott, 2010

principle: Conflict as the engine of a story
definition: Audiences connect more with a real problem, setback or challenge than with a polished success story alone; showing the struggle makes a creator or brand feel approachable and human, not just impressive.
video_application: In a Reel or Short, show the messy middle — a mistake, a doubt, a hard choice — before the payoff, instead of jumping straight to the finished result.
source: Schröder, Storytelling: A Strategic Approach (2015) (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach Towards Compelling and Meaningful Stories, Monique Schröder, 2015

definition: A story earns trust when it uses specific, real details from an actual experience rather than invented or overly polished scenes; anything that feels scripted or fictional weakens believability.
video_application: Keep small real details in a brand-collab video — an actual first reaction, an actual location, an actual message — instead of a generic staged unboxing line.
source: Schröder, Storytelling: A Strategic Approach (2015) (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach Towards Compelling and Meaningful Stories, Monique Schröder, 2015

principle: Consistency between what you say and what you do
definition: A story only holds up if it matches behavior everywhere the audience sees you — captions, comments, DMs, the product itself — not only the words in one polished video.
video_application: Only say things like 'I use this daily' in a brand-collab video if they are true, and make sure your other posts, replies and past content don't contradict it.
source: Schröder, Storytelling: A Strategic Approach (2015) (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach Towards Compelling and Meaningful Stories, Monique Schröder, 2015

principle: Treat the audience as a participant, not just a viewer
definition: People today expect to react, comment and shape a creator's or brand's story, not just receive it passively; consistently responding to that reaction builds a loyal community over time.
video_application: Turn a recurring comment or question from your audience into the topic of your next Reel or Short, and credit the commenter, so followers see their input shaping your content.
source: Schröder, Storytelling: A Strategic Approach (2015) (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach Towards Compelling and Meaningful Stories, Monique Schröder, 2015

principle: Listen to your audience before creating
definition: Before creating new content, pay attention to how your audience is already talking about you — comments, shares, their own stories about you — to check whether your last story actually landed.
video_application: Scroll your comments and saves before scripting the next video; if people keep asking the same question or misunderstanding a point, address that in your next Reel or Short.
source: Schröder, Storytelling: A Strategic Approach (2015) (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach Towards Compelling and Meaningful Stories, Monique Schröder, 2015

principle: Story matters more once competitors look alike
definition: When a product or niche is new, the offering itself can carry attention; once many creators or brands offer something similar, a distinct, consistent story becomes the main way to stand out.
video_application: If your niche (e.g. skincare, fitness) is crowded with similar creators, lean harder into your specific story and point of view in videos rather than only demonstrating the product like everyone else.
source: Schröder, Storytelling: A Strategic Approach (2015) (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: Storytelling: A Strategic Approach Towards Compelling and Meaningful Stories, Monique Schröder, 2015

principle: Origin story as an anchor for trust
definition: Sharing how and why you started — the spark, the early struggle — gives new followers or brand partners a reason to trust you beyond the current content, because they understand the ‘why’ behind it.
video_application: Post an occasional Reel or YouTube video on ‘why I started this page/channel’, including a real early struggle, to give new followers and prospective brand partners context.
source: The Power of Storytelling in Content Marketing, Breezy Content, undated online guide (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: The Power of Storytelling in Content Marketing, Breezy Content

principle: Research audience pain points before scripting
definition: Understanding the specific frustrations and needs of your followers or a brand's customers, before writing a script, makes the story land because it addresses something real rather than a generic topic.
video_application: Before filming, list the 2-3 problems your audience or the brand's customers keep mentioning in comments/DMs, then build the video's hook around solving one of them.
source: The Power of Storytelling in Content Marketing, Breezy Content, undated online guide (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: The Power of Storytelling in Content Marketing, Breezy Content

definition: Sharing a real follower's or customer's experience, in their own words, builds more trust than a creator or brand only talking about themselves, because it shows the outcome through someone else's eyes.
video_application: With the person's clear permission, include a short real clip or quote from a follower who actually used the product in a brand-collab video. Hide their personal details, don't edit their words, and skip any health, result or earnings claims the brand can't back up.
source: The Power of Storytelling in Content Marketing, Breezy Content, undated online guide (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: The Power of Storytelling in Content Marketing, Breezy Content

definition: The same underlying story can be told as a short Reel/Short, a longer YouTube video, a carousel or a caption; strong stories change length and pacing per platform without changing the core message.
video_application: Turn one brand-collab story into a punchy 30-second Reel hook and a longer YouTube walkthrough, keeping the same core message but adjusting pacing and detail for each platform.
source: The Power of Storytelling in Content Marketing, Breezy Content, undated online guide (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: The Power of Storytelling in Content Marketing, Breezy Content

definition: Comments, duets, reshares and reactions from your own audience are a source of story material, and folding them back into new content feels more genuine than only brand-originated messaging.
video_application: Turn a striking comment, duet or reaction to your last video into the opening beat of your next Reel or Short, showing you saw and responded to it.
source: The Power of Storytelling in Content Marketing, Breezy Content, undated online guide (ideas paraphrased by Influora)
further_reading: The Power of Storytelling in Content Marketing, Breezy Content

definition: Rather than targeting a broad group, picture one very specific real person (age, life stage, daily routine, worries, what they enjoy) and talk to them directly. Content made for one clear person reads as personal instead of generic.
video_application: Before scripting, write a short profile of one imagined viewer (not 'students' but 'a first-year engineering student in a Pune hostel who wants to cook cheaply and is too shy to ask seniors'). Write the hook and script as if speaking only to that person.
further_reading: Go Viral by Rachel Pedersen (free guide, rachelpedersen.com)

definition: Before creating, name the one feeling you want the viewer to have (laughter, empathy, pride, awe, nostalgia, curiosity, relief) and shape the hook, story and pacing around that one feeling instead of mixing several.
video_application: Pick one target feeling per video and check every choice (hook wording, music, pacing, camera) against it, cutting anything that pulls the other way. Aim for feelings you would be happy to be known for; avoid building videos around anger or disgust.
further_reading: Go Viral by Rachel Pedersen

steps: Grab: a short, specific first line that earns attention
Story: a brief, emotional moment or message
Call to action: one clear, named next step
video_application: A tighter alternative to PAS for very short videos and captions: go from a striking first line straight into the emotional moment, then one named action ('share this with a friend who is starting out', not just 'share').
further_reading: Go Viral by Rachel Pedersen

concept: Content mix: five kinds of video
definition: A healthy channel mixes five kinds of content: cornerstone pieces (big, time-heavy, can be cut into many smaller ones), quick tips (simple, frequent, easy to make), teaching videos (build expertise and trust), pure fun (entertainment, used now and then), and hot takes (a contrarian view that starts a conversation, used rarely).
video_application: Plan the month across all five instead of making every video the same format: an occasional cornerstone video, frequent quick-tip Reels or Shorts, regular teaching videos, some pure fun, and the odd hot take.

concept: Reorganize, rewrite, retire (getting more from old content)
definition: Three ways to get more from content you already made: reorganize (cut one big piece into several smaller ones), rewrite (refresh something that has gone out of date), and retire (take down or clearly flag something that is no longer accurate).
video_application: Cut one long YouTube video into several Reels or Shorts; add a pinned comment or a follow-up video when an older tutorial is out of date; and unlist or clearly flag a video whose claims are no longer true, so it does not mislead viewers.

concept: Judge each video by its goal
definition: Different videos have different jobs. A video meant to reach new viewers is judged by views, shares and follows; a video meant to get an action (a sign-up, a click, a purchase) is judged by that action.
video_application: Decide each video's job before posting, then judge it by the right number: don't call a discovery video a failure because it got few clicks, or a sign-up video a failure because it got fewer views.

template: Hot take: [controversial topic in your niche]. What's your opinion?
persuasion_principle: unity (invites the viewer to pick a side and belong to a camp)
